clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic SELENON variants (formerly SEPN1); it lies within the SELENON-related myopathy spectrum that also includes multiminicore disease, congenital fibre-type disproportion and Mallory-body (desmin-related) myopathy.
The hallmark is early spinal rigidity — limitation of flexion of the cervical and thoraco-lumbar spine — together with early, progressive scoliosis.
Weakness is predominantly axial and affects the neck flexors, with relatively preserved limb strength, so independent ambulation is usually retained.
Respiratory insufficiency is characteristically severe and out of proportion to limb weakness, driven by diaphragmatic weakness and nocturnal hypoventilation, and is the leading cause of morbidity.
Serum creatine kinase is normal or only mildly raised.
Muscle biopsy shows multiminicores, type-1 fibre predominance and atrophy, or fibre-type disproportion depending on the phenotype.
Reduced muscle bulk with a slender build is common, insulin resistance has been reported, and mild facial weakness may occur.
Cognition and cardiac function are typically preserved.
reference.pathophysiology: SELENON encodes selenoprotein N, an endoplasmic-reticulum glycoprotein expressed most strongly in fetal and developing muscle. It contributes to redox regulation and calcium handling, interacting with the ryanodine receptor and the sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium pump and protecting cells against oxidative stress. Loss of function disturbs calcium homeostasis and antioxidant defence within the sarcoplasmic reticulum, generating structural core lesions — regions depleted of oxidative enzyme activity and mitochondria — and impairing contractile performance. The result is a static or only slowly progressive myopathy with a striking predilection for the axial and respiratory muscles, which explains the disproportionate spinal rigidity, scoliosis and ventilatory failure.
additionalDifferentials: RYR1-related congenital myopathy (multiminicore and central core disease)
Collagen VI-related myopathy (Ullrich and Bethlem), which also causes spinal rigidity and contractures
LAMA2-related and other congenital muscular dystrophies
Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (contractures and spinal rigidity)
Other congenital myopathies with prominent respiratory involvement
additionalInvestigations: Respiratory assessment with erect and supine forced vital capacity to detect diaphragmatic weakness, and overnight oximetry with capnography
SELENON sequencing or a congenital myopathy gene panel
Muscle biopsy with oxidative enzyme histochemistry (to show minicores) and fibre typing
Muscle MRI, where the characteristic selective involvement (for example sartorius and adductors) can guide testing
Spinal imaging and orthopaedic assessment for scoliosis
Echocardiography and electrocardiography, usually normal, to document cardiac sparing
redFlags: Nocturnal hypoventilation despite preserved walking — morning headache, daytime somnolence, disturbed sleep and recurrent chest infections
A falling forced vital capacity, particularly when measured supine, indicating diaphragmatic weakness
Weight loss or failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: Muscle weakness is usually static or only slowly progressive and ambulation is typically preserved, but respiratory failure frequently develops and often requires non-invasive ventilatory support; the outlook depends chiefly on early recognition and management of hypoventilation and scoliosis.
pitfalls: The cardinal error is failing to monitor respiration because limb strength and walking are preserved — hypoventilation is insidious and can be life-threatening.
Relying on the erect vital capacity alone and missing the diaphragmatic weakness revealed by the supine measurement.
Expecting a high creatine kinase — it is frequently normal, which does not exclude the diagnosis.
Confusing it with collagen VI myopathy or Emery-Dreifuss dystrophy, which also cause spinal rigidity and contractures.
Attributing poor weight gain solely to feeding difficulty rather than to the myopathy itself.
